title: RBC membrane and enzyme disorders
covers: How the red cell membrane and metabolism keep it alive, hereditary spherocytosis and the other membrane disorders (elliptocytosis, pyropoikilocytosis, ovalocytosis, stomatocytosis), and the enzyme disorders, mainly G6PD and pyruvate kinase deficiency.

items.p: The red cell lives 120 days. It is about 8 µm wide, yet it squeezes through ~3 µm capillaries and 1–2 µm splenic slits.
It has no nucleus and no mitochondria: no protein synthesis and no oxidative phosphorylation. The biconcave disc has ~40% more surface area than a sphere of the same volume.
Survival depends on three properties:

ul: Deformability: excess surface area, normal cell volume, a flexible skeleton
Membrane stability: strong links between the lipid bilayer and the spectrin skeleton
Energy and redox balance: glycolysis for ATP, the HMP shunt for NADPH

summary.h: Membrane structure: vertical and horizontal links

items.caption: Red cell membrane: vertical and horizontal interactions (lecture slide)

items.p: Junctional complex: actin, protein 4.1, adducin, tropomodulin (glycophorin C attaches there).

ul: Glycolysis takes ~90% of glucose; net 2 ATP per glucose (PGK and pyruvate kinase steps)
ATP runs the Na⁺/K⁺ and Ca²⁺ pumps (cell volume and hydration), membrane lipid renewal, shape and deformability
HMP shunt (~10%): G6PD makes NADPH → keeps glutathione reduced (GSH) → GSH detoxifies H₂O₂ and oxidant radicals
Rapoport–Luebering shunt: 1,3-BPG → 2,3-BPG → 3-PG; 2,3-BPG lowers Hb oxygen affinity, so more O₂ reaches tissues
Methemoglobin reduction: NADH from the GAPDH step drives cytochrome b5 reductase, keeping heme iron ferrous (Fe²⁺)

items.p: Hemolytic anemia = red cells destroyed early, faster than the marrow can replace them.

ul: Intrinsic: membrane, enzymes, hemoglobin. Mostly inherited; the exception is PNH.
Extrinsic: immune (allo-, auto-, drug-induced); microangiopathic (DIC, HUS, TTP); mechanical (prosthetic valves); infections, toxins (lecturer's note: hemolysin), systemic disease

items.p: Common to all: ↑ reticulocytes, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin.
Classify by morphology first (spherocytes, elliptocytes, stomatocytes), then by the molecular defect. The lecturer marked this table "very important".

items.note: Slide 10 has a handwritten note "↑ MCHC = ↑ hemolysis". Its exact meaning is unclear (a raised MCHC is a clue to HS and xerocytosis, but it does not measure how much hemolysis there is). Not tested; worth asking the lecturer.

ul: HE: ~1 in 2,000–4,000, more common in malaria regions (West Africa); transient neonatal poikilocytosis may occur
HPP: cells fragment at lower temperatures than normal (thermal instability); transfusions; splenectomy often helps
SAO: Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines, Papua New Guinea; little or no hemolysis; only heterozygotes are common
Xerocytosis (the most common stomatocytosis): mild compensated hemolysis, perinatal edema or hydrops, pseudohyperkalemia, iron overload out of proportion to transfusions
Splenectomy is contraindicated in stomatocytosis: high risk of severe venous and arterial thrombosis, little benefit. Exclude it before any splenectomy for "HS".

summary.h: Hereditary spherocytosis: cause and clinical picture

items.p: The most common inherited membrane disorder: 1 in 2,000–5,000 births, highest in Northern Europe and Japan.
Sequence: vertical defect → membrane lost as microvesicles → spherocyte (↓ surface-to-volume, ↑ MCHC) → trapped in the splenic cords ("conditioning" worsens damage) → extravascular hemolysis.

ul: Neonatal jaundice may be the first sign; anemia often worsens in the first months of life
Classic triad: anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly; family history positive in ~75%
Gallstones: pigment stones; risk rises with age and with co-inherited Gilbert syndrome
Rarer: leg ulcers, extramedullary hematopoiesis, growth delay

table: Consider at school age, before puberty

items.p: Typical picture (hemolysis, spherocytes, MCHC often > 36 g/dL, ↑ RDW, DAT negative) plus a family history needs no further testing (BSH).
When atypical:

ul: EMA binding (flow cytometry): ↓ eosin-5-maleimide binding to band 3; high sensitivity and specificity; the test of choice
Osmotic gradient ektacytometry: deformability profile; separates HS, HE/HPP and stomatocytosis
Incubated osmotic fragility: classic but less sensitive; abnormal in any spherocytosis
NGS panel: unclear or severe cases, recessive forms, before splenectomy if unclear

items.p: Spherocytes are not specific: autoimmune hemolysis, ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn, burns, clostridial sepsis, snake, spider or scorpion venoms. Check the DAT.
Treatment:

ul: Folic acid in moderate and severe disease; transfusion as needed (infancy, crises)
Cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones, can be combined with splenectomy
Splenectomy corrects the anemia in most patients, but spherocytes remain. Partial splenectomy is an option in younger children.

Before: vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib, ideally ≥ 2 weeks before. After: penicillin prophylaxis; fever is an emergency (overwhelming post-splenectomy infection). Risks: sepsis, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension.

items.p: Case 1 (slide 21): a 6-year-old boy with jaundice during viral illnesses, father with a cholecystectomy at 30, spleen 3 cm, Hb 9.8, MCHC 37.5, retics 7%, DAT negative, small dense cells = moderate HS.
Lecturer's note: know the three groups, not every enzyme.

table: PK (AR, most common glycolytic defect); GPI (second); PFK with myopathy; TPI with severe neuromuscular disease; PGK is X-linked
G6PD (X-linked, most common enzyme defect); glutathione synthetase ± 5-oxoprolinuria
Pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase (basophilic stippling); adenosine deaminase excess (AD, ↓ ATP)

items.p: Suspect an enzyme defect: chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia (CNSHA) or episodic hemolysis, DAT negative, normal membrane tests, smear often nonspecific.
Testing pitfalls:

ul: Reticulocytosis: young cells have more enzyme, so results look falsely normal
Recent transfusion: donor cells mask the defect; wait ~3 months or test the parents
Confirm with a quantitative assay, then molecular testing
Lecturer's note: never test the patient during an acute episode

items.p: G6PD is the red cell's only source of NADPH (glucose-6-phosphate → 6-phosphogluconate). Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate GSH; glutathione peroxidase turns H₂O₂ into water. Mature cells cannot make new enzyme, so activity falls with age.
Oxidant stress → Hb denatured → Heinz bodies → the spleen removes them → bite and blister cells; membrane damage → intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

ul: > 400 million affected; highest where malaria was endemic (carriers resist severe P. falciparum); Lebanon ~2.1% of newborns

X-linked (Xq28), > 200 variants, mostly missense. Hemizygous males; heterozygous females range from normal to fully deficient because of lyonization (lecturer's note: lyonization can also make a female carrier of hemophilia bleed)

table: Middle East (incl. Lebanon), S. Europe, India

items.p: WHO 2022: A < 20% with chronic hemolysis (CNSHA) · B < 45%, acute hemolysis with triggers · C 60–150%, no hemolysis · U uncertain. Older classes I–V are still in textbooks.
Presentations (most people are asymptomatic for life without a trigger):

ul: Neonatal jaundice from day 2–3; a major cause of kernicterus; reduced bilirubin conjugation contributes; worse with Gilbert (UGT1A1) variants
Acute hemolysis hours to 2–3 days after a trigger: pallor, fever, back pain, jaundice, cola urine; self-limited as enzyme-rich young cells replace old ones
CNSHA: rare (class A), lifelong hemolysis

table: Pneumonia, viral hepatitis, gastroenteritis, typhoid; also DKA
Primaquine, tafenoquine (malaria), dapsone; rasburicase, pegloticase; methylene blue; nitrofurantoin, sulfamethoxazole (lecturer: sulfa never); phenazopyridine
Fava beans (vicine, convicine); naphthalene (mothballs); henna on neonates

items.p: Diagnosis: bite and blister cells, Heinz bodies, hemoglobinuria (dipstick blood +, few RBCs), DAT negative.

ul: Quantitative spectrophotometric assay: gold standard; also finds heterozygous females
Fluorescent spot test: screening; misses many heterozygous females
Point-of-care quantitative tests: before primaquine or tafenoquine
Molecular testing: identifies the variant; females, after transfusion, family screening
Pitfall: activity can read normal during or just after hemolysis; repeat 2–3 months later

items.p: Management: prevention is the treatment (written list of unsafe drugs and foods; test before primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone, rasburicase; neonatal screening). Acute: stop the trigger, hydrate to protect the kidneys, transfuse if severe. Neonates: early phototherapy, exchange if severe.
Case 2 (slide 34): favism with a normal G6PD assay during the episode: falsely normal; repeat in 2–3 months, or test the mother (the father passes his X only to daughters).

PK makes the last ATP of glycolysis (phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate + ATP). Deficiency: ↓ ATP → Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails → K⁺ and water leak out → dehydrated, rigid echinocytes → destroyed in the spleen (and liver).
Upstream 2,3-BPG builds up → right shift of the O₂ curve → patients tolerate the anemia better than the Hb suggests.

ul: PKLR gene (1q21), red cell and liver isoenzymes; AR, > 300 variants
~1 in 20,000 in white populations; more with founder variants (Amish) and consanguinity
Spectrum: compensated hemolysis in adults to fetal hydrops; neonatal jaundice; chronic anemia, splenomegaly, gallstones; aplastic and hemolytic crises
Iron overload even without transfusions (ineffective erythropoiesis, low hepcidin)

items.p: Diagnosis: DAT-negative CNSHA with normal membrane tests and G6PD; quantitative PK activity compared with another age-dependent enzyme (e.g. hexokinase); test the parents if just transfused; confirm with PKLR sequencing.
Treatment:

ul: Folic acid; transfuse by symptoms and growth, not Hb alone; monitor ferritin and liver MRI, chelate
Splenectomy raises Hb ~1–3 g/dL; reticulocytes paradoxically rise; vaccinate; thrombosis risk
Mitapivat: oral PK activator, adults (2022), the first disease-modifying drug; little benefit when neither variant is missense
Cure: stem cell transplant in selected cases; gene therapy in trials

items.p: Case 3 (slide 38): a girl of first-cousin parents, transfusion dependent, DAT negative, normal EMA, osmotic fragility, G6PD and Hb electrophoresis, a few echinocytes = PK deficiency.

Approach to DAT-negative hereditary hemolysis (slide 40): spherocytes → EMA, ektacytometry (HS); elliptocytes or fragments → ektacytometry, spectrin studies (HE/HPP); targets, stomatocytes → ektacytometry, PIEZO1/KCNN4 (stomatocytosis); bite cells or nonspecific → G6PD, then PK assays. Still unexplained: unstable Hb studies and an NGS panel.

cards.q: Vertical versus horizontal membrane interactions: proteins and result of a defect
cards.a: Vertical (band 3, ankyrin, 4.2, β-spectrin): vesicle loss → spherocytes (HS). Horizontal (spectrin self-association, spectrin–actin–4.1): instability → elliptocytes, fragments (HE, HPP).

cards.q: What does G6PD-derived NADPH do in the red cell?
cards.a: Keeps glutathione reduced (GSH), which detoxifies H₂O₂ and oxidant radicals

cards.q: Rapoport–Luebering shunt: product and effect
cards.a: 2,3-BPG; lowers Hb O₂ affinity so more O₂ is released to tissues

cards.q: Intravascular versus extravascular hemolysis: urine and smear
cards.a: Intravascular: hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria; bite/blister cells, schistocytes. Extravascular: no Hb, ↑ urobilinogen; spherocytes.

cards.q: Intrinsic red cell defect that is acquired, not inherited
cards.a: PNH

cards.q: HS: inheritance
cards.a: ~75% autosomal dominant; the rest recessive or de novo

cards.q: HS: most often affected protein
cards.a: Ankyrin (~50%), then band 3 (~25%), β-spectrin (~20%)

cards.q: HS: why does splenectomy help if the spherocytes remain?
cards.a: It removes the main site of destruction, greatly prolonging red cell survival

cards.q: HS: three crises and their causes
cards.a: Hemolytic (viral infection); aplastic (parvovirus B19); megaloblastic (folate deficiency)

cards.q: HS: most common severity grade
cards.a: Moderate (~60–70%): Hb 8–12, retics > 6%, bilirubin > 2

cards.q: HS: timing of splenectomy
cards.a: Severe: indicated, delay to ≥ 6 years; moderate: consider at school age, before puberty

cards.q: HS: test of choice when the picture is atypical
cards.a: EMA binding (↓ eosin-5-maleimide binding to band 3) by flow cytometry

cards.q: HS: when is no further testing needed?
cards.a: Typical picture (spherocytes, ↑ MCHC, DAT negative) plus a family history (BSH)

cards.q: Causes of spherocytes other than HS
cards.a: Autoimmune hemolysis, ABO HDN, burns, clostridial sepsis, snake/spider/scorpion venoms (check the DAT)

cards.q: Before and after splenectomy
cards.a: Before: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines ≥ 2 weeks ahead. After: penicillin prophylaxis; fever is an emergency.

cards.q: Membrane disorder in which splenectomy is contraindicated, and why
cards.a: Hereditary stomatocytosis: high risk of severe venous and arterial thrombosis, little benefit

cards.q: Dehydrated stomatocytosis (xerocytosis): genes and clues
cards.a: PIEZO1 gain-of-function or KCNN4 (Gardos); ↑ MCHC, target cells, pseudohyperkalemia, perinatal edema, iron overload

cards.q: Southeast Asian ovalocytosis: defect and clinical point
cards.a: Band 3 27-bp deletion (SLC4A1); little or no hemolysis; protects against severe malaria

cards.q: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis
cards.a: AR biallelic spectrin defects; fragments, microspherocytes, very low MCV; cells fragment at low temperature

cards.q: Three groups of red cell enzyme disorders
cards.a: Glycolysis (energy); HMP shunt and glutathione (oxidant defense); nucleotide metabolism

cards.q: Most common glycolytic defect versus most common enzyme defect
cards.a: PK deficiency (AR) versus G6PD deficiency (X-linked)

cards.q: Why can an enzyme assay be falsely normal?
cards.a: Reticulocytosis (young cells have more enzyme) or recent transfusion (wait ~3 months or test the parents)

cards.q: G6PD: what happens under oxidant stress?
cards.a: Hb denatures → Heinz bodies → spleen removes them → bite/blister cells; intravascular and extravascular hemolysis

cards.q: G6PD A− versus Mediterranean
cards.a: A−: Africa, ~10–15%, mild self-limited. Mediterranean: Middle East incl. Lebanon, < 5%, severe, favism.

cards.q: G6PD WHO 2022 classes A and B
cards.a: A: < 20% with chronic hemolysis (CNSHA). B: < 45%, acute hemolysis with triggers.

cards.q: G6PD triggers: most common, and key drugs
cards.a: Infection. Drugs: primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone, rasburicase, methylene blue, nitrofurantoin, sulfamethoxazole

cards.q: G6PD: gold standard test, and the screening test's weakness
cards.a: Quantitative spectrophotometric assay; the fluorescent spot test misses many heterozygous females

cards.q: G6PD assay normal during acute hemolysis: what next?
cards.a: May be falsely normal; repeat in 2–3 months (or test the mother)

cards.q: PK deficiency: why do patients tolerate anemia well?
cards.a: ↑ 2,3-BPG shifts the O₂ curve right, releasing more O₂ to tissues

cards.q: PK deficiency: why iron overload without transfusion?
cards.a: Ineffective erythropoiesis with low hepcidin

cards.q: PK deficiency: effect of splenectomy
cards.a: Hb rises ~1–3 g/dL, fewer transfusions; reticulocytes paradoxically rise

cards.q: Mitapivat
cards.a: Oral PK activator for adults (2022); first disease-modifying drug; little benefit if neither variant is missense

questions.stem: The mature red cell has no mitochondria. Which pathway supplies its ATP?
questions.explanation: With no nucleus or mitochondria, the red cell makes no protein and has no oxidative phosphorylation; glycolysis supplies its ATP (net 2 per glucose). B: Needs mitochondria. C: Makes NADPH, not ATP. D: Makes 2,3-BPG and bypasses an ATP-generating step. E: Needs mitochondria.

questions.stem: An 8 µm red cell must pass through which narrowest gap in the circulation?
questions.explanation: The red cell (~8 µm, lifespan 120 days) passes ~3 µm capillaries and 1–2 µm splenic slits. A: Narrow, but the splenic slits are narrower. B: Not the narrowest passage. C: Wider than the cell. E: Red cells do not pass these.

questions.stem: What gives the biconcave red cell its reserve for deformation?

options.A: Volume ~40% above that of a sphere of equal surface area
options.B: Surface area equal to that of a sphere of equal volume
options.C: Surface area ~10% above that of a sphere of equal volume
options.D: A rigid spectrin lattice that resists bending
options.E: Surface area ~40% above that of a sphere of equal volume

questions.explanation: The biconcave disc has ~40% more surface area than a sphere of the same volume: excess area, normal volume and a flexible skeleton give deformability. A: The excess is surface area, not volume. B: The disc has ~40% more. C: About 40%. D: The skeleton must be flexible.

questions.stem: Red cell survival depends on three properties. Which one fails first in pyruvate kinase deficiency?

options.A: Redox balance from the HMP shunt

questions.explanation: The three properties are deformability, membrane stability, and energy and redox balance. PK deficiency cuts ATP from glycolysis. A: That fails in G6PD deficiency. B: That fails in HS. D: That fails in HE and HPP. E: Lost secondarily in spherocytes.

questions.stem: Which protein helps link band 3 to the spectrin skeleton in the vertical axis?
questions.explanation: Vertical: band 3, ankyrin, protein 4.2, β-spectrin. Defect → membrane lost as vesicles → spherocytes. A: Part of the actin junction, not the vertical link. C: Junctional complex. D: Horizontal and junctional. E: Junctional complex.

questions.stem: A defect in spectrin self-association mainly produces which red cell shape?
questions.explanation: Horizontal interactions (spectrin self-association, spectrin–actin–protein 4.1) give the skeleton strength; defects → mechanical instability → elliptocytes and fragments (HE, HPP). A: Vertical defects. B: Cation leak disorders. C: Xerocytosis, thalassemia, liver disease. E: PK deficiency.

questions.stem: Which protein belongs to the junctional complex of the red cell skeleton?
questions.explanation: Junctional complex: actin, protein 4.1, adducin, tropomodulin; glycophorin C attaches there. A: Vertical linker. B: Transmembrane anchor. D: Vertical linker. E: Transmembrane protein.

questions.stem: About what share of red cell glucose enters the hexose monophosphate shunt?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis takes ~90% (net 2 ATP per glucose); the HMP shunt ~10%. B: About 10%. C: That share goes through glycolysis. D: About 10%. E: About 10%.

questions.stem: Each is an ATP-dependent function of the red cell EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: ATP runs the Na⁺/K⁺ and Ca²⁺ pumps (volume, hydration), membrane lipid renewal, and shape. Glutathione is kept reduced by NADPH. A: Uses ATP. B: Uses ATP. C: Uses ATP. D: Uses ATP.

questions.stem: An oxidant drug raises H₂O₂ inside red cells. Which molecule is used to detoxify it?
questions.explanation: G6PD makes NADPH; NADPH keeps glutathione reduced (GSH); GSH detoxifies H₂O₂ via glutathione peroxidase. A: Must be reduced first. C: Drives methemoglobin reduction. D: Lowers oxygen affinity. E: Methemoglobin reduction.

questions.stem: A patient's red cells contain more 2,3-BPG than normal. What happens to hemoglobin?

options.B: It binds carbon monoxide more avidly

questions.explanation: The Rapoport–Luebering shunt makes 2,3-BPG (1,3-BPG → 2,3-BPG → 3-PG), which lowers Hb oxygen affinity so more O₂ is released. B: Not an effect of 2,3-BPG. C: Unrelated. D: Oxidant damage. E: HbS.

questions.stem: Which enzyme keeps heme iron ferrous, driven by NADH from the GAPDH step?
questions.explanation: NADH from glycolysis drives cytochrome b5 reductase, keeping heme iron Fe²⁺. A: Uses NADPH for glutathione. B: Removes H₂O₂. D: Makes NADPH. E: Makes ATP.

questions.stem: Which intrinsic red cell disorder is acquired rather than inherited?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic defects (membrane, enzymes, hemoglobin) are mostly inherited; the exception is PNH. A: Inherited. B: Inherited. C: Inherited. D: Inherited.

questions.stem: A patient with clostridial sepsis develops brisk hemolysis from a bacterial hemolysin. How is this hemolysis classified?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic causes: immune, microangiopathic (DIC, HUS, TTP), mechanical (valves), infections and toxins (hemolysins), systemic disease. A: The cell is normal; the toxin is outside it. B: The cell is normal. C: The cell is normal. E: That is prosthetic valves.

questions.stem: Which finding is shared by intravascular and extravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Common to all hemolysis: ↑ reticulocytes, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin. A: Intravascular. C: Intravascular. D: Intravascular. E: Extravascular.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has dark urine a day after eating fava beans. His plasma is pink and haptoglobin is undetectable. Which urine finding appears several days later?
questions.explanation: Intravascular hemolysis: free plasma Hb ↑, haptoglobin absent, hemoglobinuria and later hemosiderinuria (tubular cells shed iron). A: The extravascular pattern. B: Glomerular bleeding. C: Hemolysis raises indirect bilirubin. D: Muscle injury.

questions.stem: A boy with hereditary spherocytosis is jaundiced. What does his urine show?
questions.explanation: Extravascular hemolysis (spleen and liver macrophages): no free Hb, haptoglobin normal or ↓, urine has no Hb but ↑ urobilinogen. A: Intravascular. B: Intravascular. C: Hemolysis raises indirect bilirubin. E: Glomerular bleeding.

questions.stem: How are inherited red cell membrane disorders classified first?

options.A: By red cell morphology on the smear
options.B: By the molecular defect on sequencing
options.C: By the result of EMA binding

questions.explanation: Classify by morphology first (spherocytes, elliptocytes, stomatocytes), then by the molecular defect. B: The second step. C: A test for HS. D: Abnormal in any spherocytosis. E: Morphology comes first.

questions.stem: A child has typical hereditary spherocytosis. Both parents have normal blood counts and smears. What best explains this?

options.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance from the father

questions.explanation: ~75% of HS is autosomal dominant; the rest is recessive or de novo. A: He would usually be affected. B: HS is not X-linked. D: Applies to X-linked genes. E: Not a mechanism of HS.

questions.stem: A healthy man from West Africa has 40% elliptocytes on a routine smear and a normal hemoglobin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HE: horizontal defects (α-spectrin most), mostly AD, ~1 in 2,000–4,000, more common in malaria regions (West Africa); most asymptomatic; > 25% elliptocytes. A: Severe, with very low MCV. C: Southeast Asia; stomatocytic ovalocytes. D: Spherocytes. E: Target cells, few stomatocytes.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has severe hemolysis, an MCV of 55 fL, and fragments, microspherocytes and bizarre poikilocytes. Both parents have mild elliptocytosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HPP: biallelic spectrin defects (AR), fragments, microspherocytes, very low MCV; cells fragment at lower temperatures than normal. B: No fragments or bizarre poikilocytes. C: Little or no hemolysis. D: High MCV. E: Not a membrane disorder; parents would be carriers.

questions.stem: What happens to red cells in hereditary pyropoikilocytosis when they are heated?

options.B: They swell and lyse in hypotonic saline
options.D: They fragment at a lower temperature
options.E: They lose potassium through a leak

questions.explanation: HPP cells are thermally unstable; transfusions are needed and splenectomy often helps. A: HS. B: Osmotic fragility. C: HbS. E: Stomatocytosis.

questions.stem: A man from Papua New Guinea has rigid oval stomatocytic cells and no anemia. Which defect is most likely?
questions.explanation: Southeast Asian ovalocytosis: band 3 27-bp deletion (SLC4A1), AD; rigid stomatocytic ovalocytes, little or no hemolysis. A: Xerocytosis. B: HS. D: HE. E: Overhydrated stomatocytosis.

questions.stem: Why is Southeast Asian ovalocytosis common in Malaysia and the Philippines?

options.D: It confers resistance to oxidant drugs

questions.explanation: SAO protects against severe malaria; only heterozygotes are common. A: Malaria. B: Autosomal dominant. C: Heterozygotes only are common. D: Not stated.

questions.stem: What is the basic defect in hereditary stomatocytosis?

options.B: Abnormal membrane permeability to Na⁺ and K⁺

questions.explanation: Hereditary stomatocytosis: abnormal Na⁺/K⁺ permeability changes cell water content (dehydrated or overhydrated). A: HS. C: HE. D: PK deficiency. E: G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has mild compensated hemolysis, MCHC 37 g/dL and target cells. He had perinatal edema. Serum potassium is 6.2 mmol/L with a normal ECG, and ferritin is high though he was never transfused. Which gene is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Dehydrated stomatocytosis (xerocytosis), the most common form: PIEZO1 gain-of-function or KCNN4; ↑ MCHC, targets, perinatal edema, pseudohyperkalemia, iron overload out of proportion to transfusions. A: Overhydrated: low MCHC, many stomatocytes. B: Southeast Asian ovalocytosis. C: PK deficiency: echinocytes. E: Bite cells.

questions.stem: Which red cell index is expected with a gain-of-function variant of the Gardos channel (KCNN4)?
questions.explanation: KCNN4 (Gardos channel) variants cause dehydrated stomatocytosis: cells lose water, so MCHC rises. A: Hemolysis is compensated. B: Overhydrated stomatocytosis. D: HPP. E: Not the expected change.

questions.stem: A child has hemolysis, MCV 112 fL, MCHC 29 g/dL and many stomatocytes. Which gene is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Overhydrated stomatocytosis: rare, RHAG variants; ↑ MCV, ↓ MCHC, many stomatocytes. A: Dehydrated: high MCHC. C: Dehydrated: high MCHC. D: Ovalocytosis. E: PK deficiency.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old labelled as having HS has hemolysis, a high MCHC, and target cells with a few stomatocytes. A splenectomy is planned. Why is splenectomy contraindicated?

options.B: High risk of rebound hemolysis in the liver

questions.explanation: Stomatocytosis: splenectomy carries a high risk of severe venous and arterial thrombosis with little benefit. Exclude it before any splenectomy for "HS". B: Not the stated reason. C: Not the stated reason. D: Not relevant. E: Not the stated reason.

questions.stem: Echinocytes appear on the smear after splenectomy. Which disorder do they point to?
questions.explanation: PK deficiency: smear nonspecific; echinocytes, especially after splenectomy. A: Bite cells, Heinz bodies. B: Spherocytes. C: Elliptocytes. D: Targets, few stomatocytes.

questions.stem: Which stain shows Heinz bodies?
questions.explanation: Heinz bodies (denatured Hb, G6PD deficiency) need a supravital stain. B: Heinz bodies are not seen on routine stains. C: Shows iron. D: Glycogen. E: Bacteria.

questions.stem: In which populations is hereditary spherocytosis most prevalent?

options.E: The Amish and other founder groups

questions.explanation: HS: 1 in 2,000–5,000 births, highest in Northern Europe and Japan; the most common inherited membrane disorder. A: G6PD deficiency and HE regions. C: SAO. D: G6PD Mediterranean. E: PK deficiency.

questions.stem: Which protein is most often defective in hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation: HS proteins: ankyrin ~50%, band 3 ~25%, β-spectrin ~20%, α-spectrin ~5%, protein 4.2 ~5%. A: Second (~25%). B: Third (~20%). C: ~5%; severe recessive HS. D: ~5%; mainly Japan.

questions.stem: A child with severe HS has two unaffected parents who each carry one variant. Which protein is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: α-spectrin defects cause severe, recessive HS; protein 4.2 defects are seen mainly in Japan. A: Usually dominant. B: Usually dominant. D: HE. E: Mainly in Japan.

questions.stem: In hereditary spherocytosis, how does the spherocyte form?
questions.explanation: Vertical defect → membrane lost as microvesicles → spherocyte (↓ surface-to-volume, ↑ MCHC) → trapped in the splenic cords → extravascular hemolysis. A: Stomatocytosis. B: G6PD deficiency. C: PK deficiency. E: Schistocytes.

questions.stem: After splenectomy for HS, a child's hemoglobin becomes normal. What does the smear now show?
questions.explanation: Splenectomy removes the main site of destruction, so survival rises, but the defect persists and spherocytes remain. B: Not expected. C: Not expected. D: PK deficiency. E: G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old boy, whose father has HS, needs phototherapy for jaundice. His hemoglobin is normal for age. What should the parents expect?

options.A: Iron deficiency develops in the first weeks
options.B: Anemia often worsens over the first months
options.C: An aplastic crisis is likely in the first weeks
options.D: Splenectomy will be needed before age 1

questions.explanation: Neonatal jaundice may be the first sign of HS; anemia often worsens in the first months; top-up transfusions may be needed in the first year. A: Not the expected course. C: Needs parvovirus infection. D: Delay to ≥ 6 years if possible. E: Risk rises with age.

questions.stem: A child has anemia, jaundice and splenomegaly with spherocytes. In about what share of HS patients is the family history positive?
questions.explanation: Classic triad: anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly; positive family history in ~75%. A: About 75%. B: About 75%. C: About 75%. D: About 75%.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with mild HS has gallstones, and her bilirubin is higher than her hemolysis explains. Which co-inherited condition is most likely?
questions.explanation: HS gallstones are pigment (bilirubin) stones; risk rises with age and with co-inherited Gilbert syndrome. A: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. B: Iron overload. C: Episodic hemolysis, not this. E: Not linked to HS.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with HS has fever, then sudden pallor. Hemoglobin has fallen from 10 to 5 g/dL, reticulocytes are 0.2%, and jaundice is no worse. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Aplastic crisis: parvovirus B19 halts erythropoiesis; reticulocytes ↓ and Hb falls sharply. A: Gradual, megaloblastic. B: Jaundice and spleen would increase; reticulocytes high. D: Reticulocytes would be high. E: Conjugated jaundice, no anemia.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with HS, taking no supplements, has slowly worsening anemia with macrocytes and a falling reticulocyte count. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic crisis: high red cell turnover (pregnancy, growth) uses up folate. A: Microcytic. B: Sudden. C: HS uses up folate. D: Reticulocytes would be high.

questions.stem: Each is a recognized complication of severe HS EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rarer HS features: leg ulcers, extramedullary hematopoiesis, growth delay in severe disease. Bite cells are G6PD. A: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: A child with HS has Hb 10 g/dL, reticulocytes 8% and bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL. How severe is the disease?
questions.explanation: Moderate HS: Hb 8–12, retics > 6%, bilirubin > 2; the most common grade (~60–70%). A: Normal Hb, retics < 3%. B: Retics 3–6%, bilirubin 1–2. D: Hb 6–8, retics > 10%, bilirubin > 3. E: Not a grade used.

questions.stem: Which grade of HS has Hb 11–15 g/dL, reticulocytes 3–6% and bilirubin 1–2 mg/dL?
questions.explanation: Mild HS: Hb 11–15, retics 3–6%, bilirubin 1–2; ~20–30% of patients; splenectomy usually not needed. B: Normal Hb, retics < 3%. C: Hb 8–12, retics > 6%. D: Hb 6–8, retics > 10%. E: Not a grade used.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with HS has Hb 7 g/dL, reticulocytes 12% and bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL. What is the plan for splenectomy?
questions.explanation: Severe HS (Hb 6–8, retics > 10%, bilirubin > 3): splenectomy indicated, delayed to ≥ 6 years if possible. A: Severe disease. B: Delay to ≥ 6 years if possible. C: Too late for severe disease. E: Indicated for severe disease.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with moderate HS is doing well at school. When is splenectomy considered?
questions.explanation: Moderate HS: consider splenectomy at school age, before puberty. A: Too early. B: Consider at school age, before puberty. D: Not the criterion. E: Not the criterion.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with severe HS needs transfusions every month. Which surgical option fits his age?
questions.explanation: Partial splenectomy is an option in younger children when total splenectomy should be delayed. B: Delay to ≥ 6 years if possible. C: Does not treat anemia. D: Not an option given. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has jaundice and pallor with viral illnesses; his father had a cholecystectomy at 30. Spleen 3 cm; Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCHC 37.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 7%, DAT negative; many small dense cells without central pallor. What further test is needed?
questions.explanation: A typical picture (spherocytes, ↑ MCHC, DAT negative) plus family history needs no further testing (BSH). This is moderate HS: folic acid; consider splenectomy at school age. A: For atypical cases. B: For atypical cases. C: Unclear or severe cases. D: For atypical cases.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has DAT-negative hemolysis with some spherocytes, a normal MCHC and no family history. Which test is preferred?
questions.explanation: When the picture is atypical, EMA binding (↓ eosin-5-maleimide binding to band 3) is the test of choice: high sensitivity and specificity. A: Less sensitive. C: Not a membrane test. D: Bite cells or nonspecific smear. E: The picture is atypical.

questions.stem: Which test separates HS, HE/HPP and stomatocytosis by their deformability profile?
questions.explanation: Osmotic gradient ektacytometry gives a deformability profile that separates HS, HE/HPP and stomatocytosis. A: Band 3 by flow cytometry. B: Abnormal in any spherocytosis. C: G6PD screen. E: Enzyme activity.

questions.stem: A woman with autoimmune hemolysis has many spherocytes. What will incubated osmotic fragility show?
questions.explanation: Incubated osmotic fragility is the classic test but less sensitive, and it is abnormal in any spherocytosis, including immune. A: Abnormal in any spherocytosis. C: Not a feature. D: Not the point; any spherocytosis is abnormal. E: Thermal instability is HPP.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with probable HS is scheduled for splenectomy, but the diagnosis is still unclear. Which test should come first?
questions.explanation: Genetic testing (NGS panel): unclear or severe cases, recessive forms, before splenectomy if unclear. A: Not part of the work-up. B: Already negative. C: G6PD screen. D: Exclude stomatocytosis first.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with no family history has anemia, jaundice and many spherocytes. The DAT is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spherocytes are not specific: autoimmune hemolysis, ABO HDN, burns, clostridial sepsis, venoms. Check the DAT. A: DAT negative. B: Targets, few stomatocytes. C: Nonspecific smear, DAT negative. E: Bite cells, DAT negative.

questions.stem: Each can cause spherocytes EXCEPT:

options.D: ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn

questions.explanation: Causes of spherocytes besides HS: autoimmune hemolysis, ABO HDN, burns, clostridial sepsis, snake, spider or scorpion venoms. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with HS has symptomatic gallstones and is booked for splenectomy. What is done about the gallbladder?

options.D: No action, as splenectomy dissolves stones

questions.explanation: Cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones; it can be combined with splenectomy. Folic acid in moderate and severe disease; transfusion as needed. B: Not the listed treatment. C: Can be combined. D: Stones remain. E: Not the listed treatment.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with severe HS is booked for elective splenectomy. When should vaccines against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib be given?

options.B: At the first postoperative clinic visit
options.E: At the first fever after surgery

questions.explanation: Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib ideally ≥ 2 weeks before; penicillin prophylaxis after. A: Ideally ≥ 2 weeks before. B: Before surgery. D: Not the stated timing. E: Before surgery.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old who had a splenectomy for HS two years ago has a temperature of 39.5 °C. What is the main concern?

options.B: An aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19
options.C: A hemolytic crisis from a viral illness
options.E: A megaloblastic crisis from folate lack

questions.explanation: After splenectomy, fever is an emergency: overwhelming post-splenectomy infection. B: Not the emergency here. C: The spleen is gone. D: A risk, but fever points to infection. E: Not suggested by fever.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old splenectomized for HS 20 years ago has progressive dyspnea; echo shows high pulmonary artery pressure. What is the link?

options.A: Pulmonary hypertension is a sign of HS relapse
options.B: Pulmonary hypertension is a late risk of splenectomy

questions.explanation: Splenectomy risks: sepsis, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension. A: Not stated. C: Not stated. D: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: To which group of red cell enzyme disorders does pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase deficiency belong?
questions.explanation: Three groups: glycolysis (energy), HMP shunt and glutathione (oxidant defense), nucleotide metabolism. A: PK, GPI, hexokinase, PFK, TPI, PGK. B: G6PD and glutathione enzymes. C: Not an enzyme group. E: Not an enzyme group here.

questions.stem: A child has chronic nonspherocytic hemolysis with coarse basophilic stippling; blood lead is normal. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase deficiency (AR): basophilic stippling. A: Echinocytes. B: Bite cells. C: 5-oxoprolinuria. D: Excess, with ↓ ATP.

questions.stem: What is the most common glycolytic enzyme defect of the red cell?
questions.explanation: PK deficiency (AR) is the most common glycolytic defect; GPI second. G6PD (HMP shunt) is the most common enzyme defect overall. B: Second most common. C: Rare. D: Most common enzyme defect, but not glycolytic. E: X-linked, rare.

questions.stem: A boy has hemolysis and myopathy. His defect is in glycolysis and is X-linked. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: PGK is the X-linked glycolytic defect (± neuro/myopathy); PFK (myopathy) and TPI (severe neuromuscular) are AR. A: Myopathy, but AR. B: Neuromuscular, but AR. C: X-linked, but HMP shunt. D: AR, no myopathy.

questions.stem: A neonate has hemolysis and metabolic acidosis with 5-oxoprolinuria. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Glutathione synthetase deficiency (AR) ± 5-oxoprolinuria. A: AR, no 5-oxoprolinuria. B: AR, no 5-oxoprolinuria. D: Glycolysis. E: X-linked; no 5-oxoprolinuria.

questions.stem: A child has chronic hemolysis, a negative DAT, no spherocytes, and normal EMA binding and osmotic fragility. Which category is most likely?
questions.explanation: Suspect an enzyme defect: CNSHA or episodic hemolysis, DAT negative, normal membrane tests, smear often nonspecific. A: EMA and osmotic fragility would be abnormal. B: DAT negative. C: Schistocytes. E: Considered only if enzymes are normal.

questions.stem: A boy with reticulocytes of 15% has PK activity at the low end of normal. Why can this mislead?

options.B: Young cells have more enzyme activity

questions.explanation: Reticulocytosis makes enzyme results look falsely normal. PK is compared with another age-dependent enzyme (hexokinase) to correct for this. A: No transfusion is mentioned. C: They have more. D: Donor cells raise it. E: Not a mechanism.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with chronic hemolysis was transfused 3 weeks ago. Her PK assay is normal. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: Recent transfusion: donor cells mask the defect; wait ~3 months or test the parents; confirm with a quantitative assay, then molecular testing. A: Donor cells mask the defect. B: Wait ~3 months. C: Not needed. E: Same problem after transfusion.

questions.stem: A boy is admitted with acute hemolysis after an infection, and an enzyme defect is suspected. When should the enzyme assay be done?
questions.explanation: The patient should not be tested during an acute episode: old deficient cells are gone and reticulocytes are enzyme-rich. Repeat 2–3 months later. B: Do not test during an acute episode. C: Results can read falsely normal. D: Still the acute episode. E: Test after recovery.

questions.stem: Which reaction does G6PD catalyze?
questions.explanation: G6PD: glucose-6-phosphate → 6-phosphogluconate, reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH, the red cell's only source of NADPH. A: Hexokinase. B: The next step. C: Pyruvate kinase. D: Rapoport–Luebering shunt.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts H₂O₂ to water in the red cell?
questions.explanation: Glutathione reductase (NADPH) regenerates GSH; glutathione peroxidase uses GSH to turn H₂O₂ into water. A: Regenerates GSH using NADPH. C: Makes NADPH. D: Reduces methemoglobin. E: Makes glutathione.

questions.stem: In G6PD deficiency, why are the oldest red cells hemolyzed first?

options.A: Old cells have lost their spectrin
options.B: Old cells are coated with antibody
options.C: Mature cells cannot make new enzyme

questions.explanation: Mature red cells cannot make new enzyme, so G6PD activity falls as the cell ages. A: Not the reason. B: DAT negative. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: How do bite cells form in G6PD deficiency?

options.A: Complement punches holes in the membrane

questions.explanation: Oxidant stress → Hb denatured → Heinz bodies → the spleen removes them → bite and blister cells; membrane damage → intravascular and extravascular hemolysis. A: Not the mechanism. B: Immune spherocytes. C: Schistocytes. D: Stomatocytosis.

questions.stem: Which reaction does pyruvate kinase catalyze?
questions.explanation: PK: phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate + ATP, the final ATP-generating step. A: Lactate dehydrogenase. C: PGK. D: GPI. E: Phosphofructokinase.

questions.stem: In PK deficiency, why do red cells become rigid echinocytes?
questions.explanation: ↓ ATP → Na⁺/K⁺ pump failure → K⁺ and water leak out → dehydrated, rigid echinocytes → destroyed in the spleen (and liver). A: HS. B: G6PD deficiency. C: G6PD deficiency. E: HE.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with PK deficiency has Hb 7.5 g/dL yet plays sports with few symptoms. What explains this?
questions.explanation: Upstream intermediates, including 2,3-BPG, build up → right shift of the dissociation curve → more O₂ released, so the anemia is better tolerated. B: Not the mechanism. C: ATP is low. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Why is G6PD deficiency most frequent where malaria was endemic?

options.A: Malaria drugs select for the variant
options.B: Fava beans grow in the same regions

questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency (> 400 million, the most common enzyme defect) is highest where malaria was endemic: carriers resist severe P. falciparum. Lebanon ~2.1% of newborns. A: Not the reason. B: Not the reason. D: Not a mechanism. E: Severe P. falciparum.

questions.stem: About what share of newborns in Lebanon have G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation: Lebanon: ~2.1% of newborns. A: About 2.1%. B: About 2.1%. C: About 2.1%. D: About 2.1%.

questions.stem: Where is the G6PD gene located?
questions.explanation: G6PD gene at Xq28; > 200 disease variants, mostly missense; hemizygous males. A: Not stated. C: PKLR. D: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: Two sisters are heterozygous for the same G6PD variant. One has normal activity; the other is as deficient as her brother. What explains this?
questions.explanation: Heterozygous females range from normal to fully deficient because of random X-inactivation (lyonization); their cells are a mosaic. A: The variant is the same. B: Not stated. D: Not relevant. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: A woman whose father had hemophilia A bleeds heavily after a dental extraction; her factor VIII is 20%. What explains her bleeding?

options.C: A de novo mutation in her

questions.explanation: Lyonization can make a female carrier of an X-linked disorder, such as hemophilia, symptomatic. B: Hemophilia A is X-linked. C: She is an obligate carrier. D: Not suggested. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A boy of African descent has mild, self-limited hemolysis during pneumonia. His G6PD activity is about 12%. Which variant fits?
questions.explanation: G6PD A−: Africa, ~10–15% residual activity, mild self-limited hemolysis. A: Wild type, normal activity. B: < 5%, severe. C: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old Lebanese boy has severe hemolysis after eating fava beans. He carries the G6PD Mediterranean variant. What residual enzyme activity is typical of it?
questions.explanation: G6PD Mediterranean: Middle East (incl. Lebanon), S. Europe, India; < 5%; severe; favism. A: G6PD A−. B: Class B range, not the Mediterranean variant. C: Class C, no hemolysis. D: Old class V.

questions.stem: A man with G6PD activity of 30% has hemolysis only after triggers. Which WHO 2022 class fits?
questions.explanation: WHO 2022: A < 20% with CNSHA; B < 45%, acute hemolysis with triggers; C 60–150%; U uncertain. A: < 20% with chronic hemolysis. C: 60–150%, no hemolysis. D: Uncertain significance. E: Older system.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old has lifelong hemolysis, splenomegaly and gallstones, with flares during infections. His G6PD activity is 8%. Which WHO 2022 class fits?
questions.explanation: Class A (rare): < 20% with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, gallstones, acute flares after triggers. B: Acute hemolysis with triggers only. C: No hemolysis. D: Uncertain significance. E: Older system; 60–150%.

questions.stem: What is the usual course of G6PD deficiency?

options.D: No symptoms unless a trigger occurs

questions.explanation: Most affected people are asymptomatic for life unless exposed to a trigger. A: PK deficiency; rare class A. B: Not the usual course. C: Not usual. E: Not the usual course.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old Lebanese boy has severe, DAT-negative jaundice and is G6PD deficient. Which co-inherited variant raises his risk of kernicterus further?
questions.explanation: G6PD neonatal jaundice (day 2–3 onward) is a major cause of kernicterus; reduced bilirubin conjugation contributes; risk rises with Gilbert (UGT1A1) variants. A: Iron. B: PK deficiency. D: Xerocytosis. E: Band 3.

questions.stem: A G6PD-deficient boy starts an oxidant drug. Hemolysis begins within 2 days but stops after a week though the drug continues. Why does it stop?

options.A: The drug is metabolized to an inactive form
options.B: Young, enzyme-rich cells replace the old ones
options.C: The spleen stops removing Heinz bodies
options.E: G6PD synthesis rises in mature cells

questions.explanation: Acute hemolysis begins hours to 2–3 days after a trigger and is usually self-limited as young, enzyme-rich cells replace old ones. A: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. D: Not immune. E: Mature cells cannot make enzyme.

questions.stem: Which trigger most often precipitates hemolysis in G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation: Infections (pneumonia, viral hepatitis, gastroenteritis, typhoid) are the most common trigger; also diabetic ketoacidosis. A: Common with Mediterranean variants, but not the most common. B: A drug trigger. C: A chemical trigger. E: A drug trigger.

questions.stem: Each can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Triggers: infections and DKA; drugs (primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone, rasburicase, pegloticase, methylene blue, nitrofurantoin, sulfamethoxazole, phenazopyridine); fava beans, naphthalene, henna. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: A woman with known G6PD deficiency has a urinary infection. Which drug must be avoided?
questions.explanation: Sulfamethoxazole is on the trigger list (sulfa drugs are not to be given); nitrofurantoin and phenazopyridine are also triggers. A: Not on the trigger list. B: Not on the trigger list. D: Not on the trigger list. E: Not on the trigger list.

questions.stem: Two days after starting a urinary antibiotic, a man has dark urine and bite cells. Which drug was most likely given?
questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin is a listed trigger of G6PD hemolysis. B: Not on the trigger list. C: Not on the trigger list. D: Not on the trigger list. E: Not on the trigger list.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with leukemia and a very high uric acid is about to receive rasburicase. What is needed first?
questions.explanation: Test before primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone or rasburicase. A: Not the risk. B: Not the risk. D: Not the risk. E: Not the risk.

questions.stem: Which constituents of fava beans trigger favism?
questions.explanation: Fava (broad) beans contain vicine and convicine; favism occurs with Mediterranean variants. A: Potato alkaloids. B: Not the trigger. C: Not the trigger. E: Not the trigger.

questions.stem: A newborn has jaundice and dark urine two days after a family ceremony. Which exposure is a recognized trigger?
questions.explanation: Chemicals: naphthalene (mothballs) and henna applied to neonates. A: Not a listed trigger. B: Not a listed trigger. C: Not a trigger. D: Not a listed trigger.

questions.stem: During a G6PD hemolytic episode, the urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows few red cells. What explains this?
questions.explanation: During an episode: bite and blister cells, Heinz bodies, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, hemoglobinuria (dipstick blood +, few RBCs), polychromasia, DAT negative. B: Muscle injury. C: Red cells would be seen. D: Not detected as blood. E: Appears later, not dipstick blood.

questions.stem: Which test is the gold standard for G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation: The quantitative spectrophotometric assay is the gold standard and also identifies heterozygous females. A: Screening test. C: Before primaquine or tafenoquine. D: Shows the effect, not activity. E: Identifies the variant.

questions.stem: The sister of a G6PD-deficient boy has a normal fluorescent spot test. Why is this not reassuring?

options.A: The test misses most deficient males
options.B: The test is falsely abnormal in females
options.C: The test detects the A− variant poorly
options.D: The test misses many heterozygous females
options.E: The test reads activity in white cells

questions.explanation: The fluorescent spot test is a screen that misses many heterozygous females; a quantitative assay or molecular testing is needed. A: Its weakness is heterozygous females. B: It misses them. C: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: A patient with vivax malaria needs tafenoquine for radical cure. Which test is done first?

options.B: A peripheral smear for bite cells

questions.explanation: Point-of-care quantitative tests are used before primaquine or tafenoquine. A: Misses heterozygous females. B: Not a test of activity. C: Not relevant. D: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A G6PD-deficient boy was transfused yesterday for acute hemolysis. How can the deficiency be confirmed now?
questions.explanation: Molecular testing identifies the variant; useful in females, after transfusion, and for family screening. A: Donor cells mask the defect. B: Donor cells mask the defect. D: Not diagnostic. E: Membrane test.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has pallor and cola-colored urine 36 hours after eating fava beans: Hb 6.4 g/dL, haptoglobin undetectable, DAT negative, bite and blister cells. His G6PD assay today is normal. What is the best interpretation?
questions.explanation: During acute hemolysis the oldest, most deficient cells are gone and reticulocytes are enzyme-rich, so activity can look normal. Repeat 2–3 months later. A: Activity can read normal during hemolysis. C: Bite cells, DAT negative after fava beans. D: Acute episode after fava beans. E: The result is expected during hemolysis.

questions.stem: The same boy's family asks which parent should be tested. Who?

options.D: Neither, as it is de novo

questions.explanation: X-linked: a father passes his X only to daughters, so the mother is tested. B: He passes his X only to daughters. C: X-linked: the mother. D: Not suggested. E: Test the mother.

questions.stem: What is the main management of G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation: Prevention is the treatment: education, a written list of unsafe drugs and foods, testing before primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone, rasburicase, neonatal screening. A: Only for chronic (class A) hemolysis. B: Only in selected severe class A cases. C: Not routine. E: Mitapivat is for PK.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with G6PD deficiency has acute hemolysis during pneumonia, with Hb 8.5 g/dL and dark urine. Besides treating the infection, what is done?
questions.explanation: Acute hemolysis: stop the trigger, treat infection, hydrate to protect the kidneys from hemoglobinuria, transfuse if severe or ongoing. A: Only selected class A cases. C: Not immune. D: Not indicated. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A G6PD-deficient newborn's bilirubin is rising. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: Neonatal jaundice: close bilirubin monitoring, early phototherapy, exchange if severe. Class A chronic hemolysis: folic acid, transfusion, splenectomy in selected severe cases. B: If severe. C: Not listed. D: Not in neonates. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which gene is mutated in pyruvate kinase deficiency?
questions.explanation: PKLR (chromosome 1q21) encodes red cell (R) and liver (L) isoenzymes; AR; > 300 variants. A: Not the red cell gene. B: G6PD deficiency. C: Band 3. D: Xerocytosis.

questions.stem: In which population is PK deficiency more frequent because of a founder variant?
questions.explanation: PK deficiency: ~1 in 20,000 in white populations; higher with founder variants (Amish) and consanguinity. A: HS. B: HE, G6PD A−. D: SAO. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: What is the most severe presentation of PK deficiency?
questions.explanation: Spectrum: compensated hemolysis in adults to fetal hydrops and transfusion dependence. B: The mild end, in adults. C: Common but not the most severe. D: Chronic complication. E: Episodic.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with PK deficiency has never been transfused, yet his ferritin is 1,800 ng/mL. What explains this?
questions.explanation: PK deficiency: iron overload even without transfusions (ineffective erythropoiesis, low hepcidin). Monitor ferritin and liver MRI; chelate as needed. A: Not the stated mechanism. B: Mainly extravascular; iron is not lost this way. D: Hepcidin is low. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with first-cousin parents had an exchange transfusion at birth and is transfused every 2–3 months. Spleen 4 cm; reticulocytes 12%; DAT negative; EMA binding, osmotic fragility, G6PD and Hb electrophoresis normal; a few echinocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Severe DAT-negative nonspherocytic hemolysis, consanguinity (AR), normal membrane tests, G6PD and electrophoresis. Confirm with PK assay and PKLR sequencing. A: EMA and osmotic fragility normal. B: G6PD normal. C: Electrophoresis normal. E: DAT negative.

questions.stem: Why is PK activity compared with hexokinase activity in the same sample?

options.B: To detect a combined enzyme defect

questions.explanation: Hexokinase is another age-dependent enzyme; comparing them corrects for reticulocytosis. Confirm with PKLR sequencing. A: Test the parents or wait. B: Not the purpose. C: A separate assay. D: Not the purpose.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with PK deficiency has Hb 7.5 g/dL but grows normally and is active. What is the transfusion plan?

options.A: Transfuse to keep Hb above 8 g/dL
options.B: Transfuse if symptoms or poor growth appear

questions.explanation: Supportive care: folic acid; transfuse by symptoms and growth, not by Hb alone; monitor ferritin and liver MRI. A: Not by Hb alone. C: Not the rule. D: Not the rule. E: Not the rule.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with PK deficiency has a splenectomy. Six months later Hb has risen from 7 to 9 g/dL, and reticulocytes have risen from 12% to 40%. How is the reticulocyte rise interpreted?
questions.explanation: PK splenectomy raises Hb ~1–3 g/dL and cuts transfusions; reticulocytes paradoxically rise. Vaccinate; thrombosis risk. A: Hb has risen. B: Not needed to explain it. D: Not the situation. E: It fits PK deficiency.

questions.stem: What is mitapivat?
questions.explanation: Mitapivat: oral PK activator approved for adults (2022), the first disease-modifying drug. A: It activates PK. C: Not a chelator. D: Oral activator. E: Not its action.

questions.stem: An adult with PK deficiency carries two PKLR variants, neither of them missense. What response to mitapivat is expected?
questions.explanation: Mitapivat's benefit depends on genotype: little when neither variant is missense. Cure: stem cell transplant in selected cases; gene therapy in trials. A: Genotype limits benefit. B: Not stated. C: Not stated. D: Approved for adults.

questions.stem: A child has DAT-negative hemolysis, a nonspecific smear and normal G6PD activity. What is the next test?
questions.explanation: Bite cells or a nonspecific smear: G6PD, then PK and other enzyme assays. B: For spherocytes. C: For elliptocytes or fragments. D: For stomatocytes. E: Already negative.

questions.stem: A child with DAT-negative hemolysis has elliptocytes and fragments on the smear. Which tests are next?
questions.explanation: Elliptocytes or fragments: ektacytometry, spectrin studies, genetics → HE/HPP. A: For spherocytes. B: For bite cells or a nonspecific smear. C: For stomatocytes. E: Not this branch.

questions.stem: A child with DAT-negative hemolysis has normal membrane tests and normal G6PD and PK activity. What comes next?
questions.explanation: Still unexplained: unstable hemoglobin studies and a next-generation sequencing hemolysis panel. A: Already normal. B: Already negative. C: Not in the algorithm. D: Not in the algorithm.

questions.stem: Where does hemolysis mainly occur in PK deficiency?
questions.explanation: PK deficiency: mainly extravascular (spleen and liver). G6PD deficiency: intravascular and extravascular. A: G6PD (with extravascular). C: Ineffective erythropoiesis is a separate point. D: Not the site. E: Not the site.

questions.stem: Which hemolysis pattern fits PK deficiency?
questions.explanation: G6PD: episodic acute hemolysis after triggers, neonatal jaundice. PK: chronic hemolysis from birth. B: G6PD deficiency. C: Not stated. D: Not stated. E: From birth.
